State of the Nation 2018

By: Chwayitisa Futshane | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
with multiple investigations, parliamentary hearings, court cases and commissions of inquiries, South Africa may finally be on the brink of a truth that brings change

Unique Selling Point:
From the sweetheart resignation of Jacob Zuma as state president, to Ramaphoria and even more more resignations from cabinet, over the last 12 months, South Africa's political landscape has seen some dramatic changes. We map the changing political environment, celebrate some of our epic sporting wins and mourn the losses of some of the country's great musical and political giants.

Summary:
In December 2017, South Africa was a different country. Jacob Zuma was the ever deviant state president and the country held it's collective breath, as the ruling party headed into its highly contentious national conference.

The results were close, but Cyril Ramaphosa came out the winner and within weeks, Ramaphosa yanked the reigns of power from Zuma, to be become South Africa's new president and usher in the era of 'Ramaphoria'.

Against this background, the economy continued to contract, VAT was increased and the country entered into it's first technical recession since 2008. Under pressure, the rand ducked and dived and unemployment numbers increased as businesses continued to shed jobs.

On the sporting front, Kevin Anderson reached the final of his first major grand slam, the Springboks beat the All Blacks in New Zealand and the Proteas continued to produce some magical runs on the field.

On all fronts South Africa is a journalists dream.

Final Script


VO: Just weeks after the ANC elected Cyril Ramaphosa as the new party president at their national conference in December, narrowly beating outgoing president Jacob Zuma’s favoured candidate Dr Nkosazana Dhlamini Zuma, South Africans braced themselves for 2018.

Flooded by allegations of fraud and corruption, with state capture and public institutions like SARS and Eskom on the brink of collapse – the Zuma years had taken their toll on the country.

CLIP ONE PITYANA: 11:29 – we were in denial about the extent of corruption, we were in denial about it being championed at the very top and endorsed to the extent that no action was taken…
VO INTRO: Two years ago, political activist, Civil Society Organisation Save SA convenor and now President of Business Unity South Africa Sipho Pityana wept as he fought for a country teetering on the edge…

Now he counts the cost of the Zuma presidency.
CLIP ONE PITYANA: 11:29 The state coffers today are empty. That’s the reality. Our debt to GDP ratio now sits at almost 60 percent if you include the high levels of debt in state owned entities which are underwritten by the state, you go to 70 percent.
VO: As the new year began, it became clear Zuma had lost his iron grip on the party…the tide was turning and the emperor was exposed…
UPSOUND: ZUMA “I have therefore come to the decision to resign”…
Then Late on the 14th of February Zuma became the second elected president not to complete his term of office.

The Emperor had fallen.
Clip One DEREK: Valentines, President Zuma’s resignation, how did you feel then?

PITYANA: 08:55 – Well my wife threw the flowers I had bought for her in the bin because a greater prize was presented to all of us as a nation which was Zuma resignation. It was good for the country.
PROF BOOYSEN clip one [06:59] … It was a scorched political earth that he left behind. It really destroyed trust in the state, trust in the ANC, credibility in the ANC.
VO INTRO: PROFFESSOR SUSAN BOOYSEN is the Director of Research at the Mapungubwe Institute for Strategic Reflection – which analyses what it would take for the nation to prosper and achieve social equity.
PROF BOOYSEN: [03:38] … At best it will take decades if possible ever at all to get rid of that ghastly past and get a new future. I think in many ways South African society has changed irretrievably.
VO: Pityana warns that the party continues to underestimate the impact of the Zuma presidency….
PITYANA CLIP THREE 08:55… it’s a pity that he continues to be a major factor in SA politics and I think that ANC is still to realise how much of a blemish not only to the country and ANC that JZ is – to use him as one of their chief campaigners is an insult to the people of SA.
UPSOUND: Swearing in clip
LINK - In February Cyril Ramaphosa became the most powerful man in the country.
[Interrupt: Phakama Ramaphosa]
Expectations were high, and the excitement was palpable.




VO: But just days after Ramaphosa’s swearing in – VAT increased for the first time in 25 years.

In March petrol, diesel and paraffin followed and the ratings agencies continued to circle.

A new dawn – the President had promised – but for many people nothing really changed.
CLIP ONE
DEREK Question: Was there a false optimism after presidential switch?
PITYANA 03:36 – Yes, there was a false optimism and you could understand why cause the impact of the Zuma administration was a huge shock to society
VO INTRO JUDGE YACOOB: Retired Justice of the Constitutional Court and social activist Judge Zak Yacoob says that the problem is bigger than Zuma….
Judge Yacoob: 10:35 – … people have wishfully in my view became too euphoric and placed too much significance on the Zuma resignation and I would suggest that those people to rid the country and ANC of this cancer, is not that easy…
VO: And Pityana cautions against ordinary South Africans becoming complacent…
PITYANA CLIP ONE 01:26 – …..
… the nation suddenly went back to the notion of seeing this new president as a saviour and it had a way of demobilising effect of what we saw as an impressive civil society effort to play a part in defending the country and making sure that it stays the course in a driving the agenda for a constitutional state.



LINK: Fuel hikes, the VAT increase and an economy in decline - it’s been another difficult year for The consumer. More demands on your income and less money in your wallet…
VO: But STANDARD BANK CHIEF ECONOMIST GOOLAM BALLIM says that the political changes in the country have had a noticeable impact.
DEREK WATTS 02:35: The rand has been bruised for a few years now, how did it fare this year?
Goolam Ballim 02:41: The last five years the rand has been significantly influenced by South Africa’s volatile political cycle. It’s astonishing to believe for example that five years ago you could buy a dollar for ten rand... My sense it’s that with incremental but continuous political reforms and a further strengthening in the mandate of president Ramaphosa that rand especially in 2019 is likely to claw back some of its earlier weakness.
Derek Watts 06:53: So it’s not a totally gloomy outlook…

Goolim Ballim 06:55: I suspect we will in many years, to come look back and judge 2018 and 2019 as inflection years, years where we had political regime change…. these will be the stabilization years that then serves as the bedrock for more meaningful economic reforms in subsequent years which will propel the economy’s growth to greater heights.
VO: But it’s not just the struggling economy or the flailing rand that’s giving this president a headache.
LINK: If you take a walk in the city, thousands of people fill the streets, rushing to their next appointment and trying to get it to work on time. But the reality is, there are thousands more, sitting at home ... unemployed and desperately trying to find a way to make a living.
PITYANA CLIP TWO 08:08 – …. The critical thing which is the focus of the president today is that we must attract investment. … unless you grow the economy you will not be able to absorb labour. It’s true that growth doesn’t inevitably create employment but it is also true without growth, there can be no improvement in your employment situation.



UPSOUND: Ramaphosa “…”
LINK: From “pay back the money” to “fees must fall” - every year tends to introduce a new buzz term to our vocabulary ... and in 2018, LAND EXPROPRIATION WITHOUT COMPENSATION, captivated our collective imagination
JUDGE YACOOB: 19:25 – This is the battle between the ANC and the EFF to secure voters and the ANC understood that the EFF by making these noises about land might reduce the ANC’s vote base.
VO: Judge Yacoob believes that the ANC was backed into a corner and had to adjust its stance on land redistribution.
JUDGE YACOOB: 19:25 …..Remember that land is a very emotive issue – it is a vote catcher second to none. Neither the ANC nor the EFF is particularly interested in all the land belonging to the people. Just .. apply your mind to the question – are these people prepared to give away their own houses to the people? The answer is quite obvious.
PROF BOOYSEN Clip one [06:59] …The ANC throughout this run-up to the 2019 election, they’re trying to get their liberation rhetoric going again…But the struggle rhetoric 2018/2019 just does not have the same traction that it had before.
VO: Ballim admits that this policy poses a serious test for attracting international investment.
GOOLAM: The challenge is that we able … … to create a level of land transformation but at the same time give security to investors that industrial property, urban land, residential abodes will fall outside of the purview of expropriation possibilities.
PITYANA CLIP THREE 10:20 - Business is committed to the principal of land redistribution because we believe that property rights and land redistribution is one of the key and critical agenda items for inclusive growth…
VO: For Pityana the problem isn’t the Constitutional framework on land redistribution, but rather that land expropriation without compensation suggests a disregard for property rights, further exacerbating investor uncertainty.
PITYANA CLIP FOUR 01:00 – … It had a lot do with fears that where people have seen this happen in other countries, it starts with this and it becomes expropriation of property and it undermines property rights.
Goolam Ballim Clip one 05:56: There is no economy that has proven to be enduringly prosperous that has not hinged itself on iron clad property rights. Property rights is the cornerstone of a free market economy ... And until we get clarity on section25 people are going to be hesitant.




LINK: Under the Zuma presidency, the state capture project and the calculated destruction of the South African Revenue Services continued unhindered. Municipalities and public enterprises were brazenly looted, and law enforcement agencies looked away... Now newly appointed inquiries like the Zondo and Nugent Commissions, are just starting to show just had deeply the rot had set in.
VO: But Commissions of Inquiry have no powers to criminally charge or prosecute wrongdoers.
During the Life Esidimeni Arbitration process, it was found that over 144 mentally ill patients in the care of the state had died – many from hunger and dehydration.
But to date, not a single arrest has been made.
JUDGE JACOOB: … commissions are toothless bodies, they are appointed by the president and in the end it is the president who decides what to do about the report of that commission.
PITYANA 04:34 … the public will lose trust in what we are trying to do with these inquires unless somebody is held accountable
PROF BOOYSEN clip two [00:00] – They have been such a big part of the project of trying to get a clean-up, trying not just to get a better government, more accountable, more honest government – but to give South Africans a sense that this is a government that is actually working for them…
VO: It wasn’t just government under scrutiny this year… the extent of financial fraud at Steinhoff became evident; some major international consulting and auditing firms came under fire and VBS bank executives siphoned millions from the poor.
Pityana and Yacoob want to see wrongdoers prosecuted even as the Inquiries continue …
JUDGE YACOOB 16:05… Prosecutions and commissions could work side by side, you don’t have to wait for the one to finish before the other would happen and I would rather have that result.
PITYANA CLIP THREE 05:53 – I long for the day when the criminals who had occupied seats of power in our state system spend the time where they belong in jail. Unless that happens, crime pays.


PROMOS
10 SECONDS
VO: From the VAT increase and an economy in a technical recession…we tally up the losses, analyse the gains….and ask what’s the way forward for a country on the brink.

15 SECONDS
VO: President Cyril Ramaphosa promised a new dawn. But with a weaker economy and billions lost to state capture, for many South Africans, there’s more demand on your income and less money in your wallet. So what’s the real state of the nation?

15 SECONDS
VO: In February Cyril Ramaphosa became the most powerful man in the country.
Expectations were high, and the excitement was palpable. A new dawn he promised – and after eleven months of clawing back against state capture, is the president delivering?

30 SECONDS
DEREK: Valentines, President Zuma’s resignation, how did you feel then?
PITYANA: 08:55 – Well my wife threw the flowers I had bought for her in the bin because a greater prize was presented to all of us as a nation which was Zuma resignation.
VO: In February this year Jacob Zuma resigned as state president. But as the country celebrated, the economy remained on the brink. Eleven months later, what’s the real state of the nation?

I think in many ways South African society has changed irretrievably. VO: Pityana warns that the party continues to underestimate the impact of the Zuma presidency…. PITYANA CLIP THREE 08:55… it’s a pity that he continues to be a major factor in SA politics and I think that ANC is still to realise how much of a blemish not only to the country and ANC that JZ is – to use him as one of their chief campaigners is an insult to the people of SA. UPSOUND: Swearing in clip LINK - In February Cyril Ramaphosa became the most powerful man in the country. [Interrupt: Phakama Ramaphosa] Expectations were high, and the excitement was palpable. VO: But just days after Ramaphosa’s swearing in – VAT increased for the first time in 25 years. In March petrol, diesel and paraffin followed and the ratings agencies continued to circle. A new dawn – the President had promised – but for many people nothing really changed. CLIP ONE DEREK Question: Was there a false optimism after presidential switch? PITYANA 03:36 – Yes, there was a false optimism and you could understand why cause the impact of the Zuma administration was a huge shock to society VO INTRO JUDGE YACOOB: Retired Justice of the Constitutional Court and social activist Judge Zak Yacoob says that the problem is bigger than Zuma…. Judge Yacoob: 10:35 – … people have wishfully in my view became too euphoric and placed too much significance on the Zuma resignation and I would suggest that those people to rid the country and ANC of this cancer, is not that easy… VO: And Pityana cautions against ordinary South Africans becoming complacent… PITYANA CLIP ONE 01:26 – ….. … the nation suddenly went back to the notion of seeing this new president as a saviour and it had a way of demobilising effect of what we saw as an impressive civil society effort to play a part in defending the country and making sure that it stays the course in a driving the agenda for a constitutional state. LINK: Fuel hikes, the VAT increase and an economy in decline - it’s been another difficult year for The consumer. More demands on your income and less money in your wallet… VO: But STANDARD BANK CHIEF ECONOMIST GOOLAM BALLIM says that the political changes in the country have had a noticeable impact. DEREK WATTS 02:35: The rand has been bruised for a few years now, how did it fare this year? Goolam Ballim 02:41: The last five years the rand has been significantly influenced by South Africa’s volatile political cycle. It’s astonishing to believe for example that five years ago you could buy a dollar for ten rand... My sense it’s that with incremental but continuous political reforms and a further strengthening in the mandate of president Ramaphosa that rand especially in 2019 is likely to claw back some of its earlier weakness. Derek Watts 06:53: So it’s not a totally gloomy outlook… Goolim Ballim 06:55: I suspect we will in many years, to come look back and judge 2018 and 2019 as inflection years, years where we had political regime change…. these will be the stabilization years that then serves as the bedrock for more meaningful economic reforms in subsequent years which will propel the economy’s growth to greater heights. VO: But it’s not just the struggling economy or the flailing rand that’s giving this president a headache. LINK: If you take a walk in the city, thousands of people fill the streets, rushing to their next appointment and trying to get it to work on time. But the reality is, there are thousands more, sitting at home ... unemployed and desperately trying to find a way to make a living. PITYANA CLIP TWO 08:08 – …. The critical thing which is the focus of the president today is that we must attract investment. … unless you grow the economy you will not be able to absorb labour. It’s true that growth doesn’t inevitably create employment but it is also true without growth, there can be no improvement in your employment situation. UPSOUND: Ramaphosa “…” LINK: From “pay back the money” to “fees must fall” - every year tends to introduce a new buzz term to our vocabulary ... and in 2018, LAND EXPROPRIATION WITHOUT COMPENSATION, captivated our collective imagination JUDGE YACOOB: 19:25 – This is the battle between the ANC and the EFF to secure voters and the ANC understood that the EFF by making these noises about land might reduce the ANC’s vote base. VO: Judge Yacoob believes that the ANC was backed into a corner and had to adjust its stance on land redistribution. JUDGE YACOOB: 19:25 …..Remember that land is a very emotive issue – it is a vote catcher second to none. Neither the ANC nor the EFF is particularly interested in all the land belonging to the people. Just .. apply your mind to the question – are these people prepared to give away their own houses to the people? The answer is quite obvious. PROF BOOYSEN Clip one [06:59] …The ANC throughout this run-up to the 2019 election, they’re trying to get their liberation rhetoric going again…But the struggle rhetoric 2018/2019 just does not have the same traction that it had before. VO: Ballim admits that this policy poses a serious test for attracting international investment. GOOLAM: The challenge is that we able … … to create a level of land transformation but at the same time give security to investors that industrial property, urban land, residential abodes will fall outside of the purview of expropriation possibilities. PITYANA CLIP THREE 10:20 - Business is committed to the principal of land redistribution because we believe that property rights and land redistribution is one of the key and critical agenda items for inclusive growth… VO: For Pityana the problem isn’t the Constitutional framework on land redistribution, but rather that land expropriation without compensation suggests a disregard for property rights, further exacerbating investor uncertainty. PITYANA CLIP FOUR 01:00 – … It had a lot do with fears that where people have seen this happen in other countries, it starts with this and it becomes expropriation of property and it undermines property rights. Goolam Ballim Clip one 05:56: There is no economy that has proven to be enduringly prosperous that has not hinged itself on iron clad property rights. Property rights is the cornerstone of a free market economy ... And until we get clarity on section25 people are going to be hesitant. LINK: Under the Zuma presidency, the state capture project and the calculated destruction of the South African Revenue Services continued unhindered. Municipalities and public enterprises were brazenly looted, and law enforcement agencies looked away... Now newly appointed inquiries like the Zondo and Nugent Commissions, are just starting to show just had deeply the rot had set in. VO: But Commissions of Inquiry have no powers to criminally charge or prosecute wrongdoers. During the Life Esidimeni Arbitration process, it was found that over 144 mentally ill patients in the care of the state had died – many from hunger and dehydration. But to date, not a single arrest has been made. JUDGE JACOOB: … commissions are toothless bodies, they are appointed by the president and in the end it is the president who decides what to do about the report of that commission. PITYANA 04:34 … the public will lose trust in what we are trying to do with these inquires unless somebody is held accountable PROF BOOYSEN clip two [00:00] – They have been such a big part of the project of trying to get a clean-up, trying not just to get a better government, more accountable, more honest government – but to give South Africans a sense that this is a government that is actually working for them… VO: It wasn’t just government under scrutiny this year… the extent of financial fraud at Steinhoff became evident; some major international consulting and auditing firms came under fire and VBS bank executives siphoned millions from the poor. Pityana and Yacoob want to see wrongdoers prosecuted even as the Inquiries continue … JUDGE YACOOB 16:05… Prosecutions and commissions could work side by side, you don’t have to wait for the one to finish before the other would happen and I would rather have that result. PITYANA CLIP THREE 05:53 – I long for the day when the criminals who had occupied seats of power in our state system spend the time where they belong in jail. Unless that happens, crime pays. PROMOS 10 SECONDS VO: From the VAT increase and an economy in a technical recession…we tally up the losses, analyse the gains….and ask what’s the way forward for a country on the brink. 15 SECONDS VO: President Cyril Ramaphosa promised a new dawn. But with a weaker economy and billions lost to state capture, for many South Africans, there’s more demand on your income and less money in your wallet. So what’s the real state of the nation? 15 SECONDS VO: In February Cyril Ramaphosa became the most powerful man in the country. Expectations were high, and the excitement was palpable. A new dawn he promised – and after eleven months of clawing back against state capture, is the president delivering? 30 SECONDS DEREK: Valentines, President Zuma’s resignation, how did you feel then? PITYANA: 08:55 – Well my wife threw the flowers I had bought for her in the bin because a greater prize was presented to all of us as a nation which was Zuma resignation. VO: In February this year Jacob Zuma resigned as state president. But as the country celebrated, the economy remained on the brink. Eleven months later, what’s the real state of the nation?

metadata.Unique Selling Point: From the sweetheart resignation of Jacob Zuma as state president, to Ramaphoria and even more more resignations from cabinet, over the last 12 months, South Africa's political landscape has seen some dramatic changes. We map the changing political environment, celebrate some of our epic sporting wins and mourn the losses of some of the country's great musical and political giants.
metadata.Summary: In December 2017, South Africa was a different country. Jacob Zuma was the ever deviant state president and the country held it's collective breath, as the ruling party headed into its highly contentious national conference. The results were close, but Cyril Ramaphosa came out the winner and within weeks, Ramaphosa yanked the reigns of power from Zuma, to be become South Africa's new president and usher in the era of 'Ramaphoria'. Against this background, the economy continued to contract, VAT was increased and the country entered into it's first technical recession since 2008. Under pressure, the rand ducked and dived and unemployment numbers increased as businesses continued to shed jobs. On the sporting front, Kevin Anderson reached the final of his first major grand slam, the Springboks beat the All Blacks in New Zealand and the Proteas continued to produce some magical runs on the field. On all fronts South Africa is a journalists dream.
